newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish President Robinson rules out second term.
newsitem.headline: Irish President Robinson rules out second term.

text.p: Irish President Mary Robinson announced on Wednesday she would not stand for a second seven-year term but would like to play a role on the international stage in the area of human rights.
"It has been a difficult decision for me and I have, with great reluctance, decided not to seek a second term in office," Robinson, Ireland's first woman head of state, said in a statement.

Robinson overcame huge odds in the male-dominated world of Irish politics to win the 1990 presidential election. A lawyer, she injected vibrancy into the political process and raised Ireland's profile overseas.

"I believe that by the end of this term I will have made my contribution and that the people will give a mandate to a new president with the vision to represent them as we move into the new millennium," she said.

Robinson had been suggested as a possible United Nations secretary-general and there was speculation in Ireland that she could be offered a top U.N. human rights post, such as commissioner for refugees.
Northern Ireland Catholic politician John Hume was installed as favourite to take over when Robinson leaves office in December.
Hume, leader of the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), has been instrumental in the search for peace in the British-ruled province.
Dublin bookmakers made former prime minister Albert Reynolds the second favourite at 5/1, while Nobel literature prize winner, poet Seamus Heaney, was given odds of 12/1.
Deputy Irish opposition leader Mary O'Rourke, who had been considered a possible contender, ruled herself out after Robinson's announcement.

In her statement, Robinson thanked the Irish people for their trust and goodwill. "The unwavering support I have received as president has enabled me to contribute to the development of the office as a resource for all the people, one that is open, inclusive and tolerant," she said.
Political leaders praised the new look that Robinson brought to the presidential post, saying she symbolised a new, modern Ireland.
Deputy Prime Minister Dick Spring, who nominated his ex-Labour party colleague for the presidency in 1990, said her departure would be greeted with great sadness.

"In the seven years since her election, President Robinson has transformed the office. She has kept every promise she made, contributed to the transformation of Ireland's international image and to the development of reconciliation on the island of Ireland," he said in a statement.
Robinson, a noted orator with a deep knowledge of development issues, said she was interested in becoming involved in human rights.

"I have a real commitment, particularly in the area of human rights. I would like to continue in that area and I will be exploring the possibilities," she said. "I have given what I could and I have lots to do."
